messages.author: aa17a960edc5c28f
messages.subject: Marsh Seedeater occurrence study
parts:
Dear hmecology users, my name is Joaquin Aldabe from Uruguay. I'm conducting a study which aim is to identify factors that affect occupancy of a globally endangered tall grassland species called Marsh Seedeater Sporophila palustris (endemic to Southern Cone of South America). 

Sites were considered as 0.5 ha grassland patches along routes, and separated each other for at least 500 m (so sites are not independent; it's a unique patchy seedeater population). I already have one season dataset with 24 presence sites and about 70 absence sites. However, I did not consider imperfect detection and I suspect that false negatives may be important. So, I'm planning going back to the field this season (starting these days) and repeat each site survey, do two visits to each site (temporal replicates) and through dynamic occupancy model estimate probability of occurrence for each season as a function of covariates, considering probability of detection calculated based on this season survey and assuming there are no significant changes in observation conditions and population size. Thus, I will be able to estimate colonisation and extinction rates and assess what covariates govern them. 

This approach was built with the aid of Marc Kery, who suggested me to consult it to a wider audience. So, I would really appreciate your comments. 

All the best,
Joaquin

--
Joaquín Aldabe

Grupo Biodiversidad, Ambiente y Sociedad
Centro Universitario de la Región Este, Universidad de la República
Ruta 15 (y Ruta 9), Km 28.500, Departamento de Rocha  
                                                           
Departamento de Conservación
Aves Uruguay
BirdLife International
Canelones 1164, Montevideo

messages.subject: Re: Marsh Seedeater occurrence study
parts:
Thanks Michael! I'm going to revise those papers. Initially, I can say that I don't have as many routes as you. It's a very small population that occurs along 50 or 60 km of grasslands along the border of the route..

It's interesting that you can use spatial replicates for estimating probability of detection. 

Thanks again for your help.

Joaquin


2016-12-10 14:49 GMT-03:00 Michael Hardy <mah...@wisc.edu>:

Hi Joaquin,


Have you considered the approach described by Hines et al. 2010 & 2014 (attached)? I've used that model for a grassland bird dataset where we conducted occupancy surveys along 81 survey routes with 4 stations on each route (~800m spacing) and I found it to be a good fit for our study design. The route is treated as a site and the stations are treated as replicate surveys to estimate detection probability, so you only need to survey each route once per field season. In addition to the standard parameters for a multi-season occupancy model (psi,p,epsilon,gamma), the model has 2 additional parameters that account for spatial autocorrelation among the spatial replicates. 


Hope this helps!


Michael

messages.author: aa17a960edc5c28f
messages.subject: Re: Marsh Seedeater occurrence study
parts:
Interesting model! I'll revise my data to see if I can consider broader sites. That would allow me to save extra sampling. Something that sounded nice to me with the dynamic occupancy model is the estimation of colonization and extinction rates, which I guess are not calculated with Hines model. 
Cheers,
Joaquin

2016-12-10 15:26 GMT-03:00 Michael Hardy <mah...@wisc.edu>:

No problem, glad to help!


We were sampling a large area (~450,000 ha), but the model should work for smaller areas too if you can separate your study area into larger habitat "blocks" that you could consider independent of one another (where each block has at least 2 of the 0.5ha grassland patches you described). Then use those "blocks" as your "sites" (independent) and the smaller grassland patches as your repeat surveys (not independent). The Hines model will give you occupancy at the "site" level and also conditional occupancy probability at the "local" level (i.e., probability of the smaller patch within the block being occupied, given that the larger block is occupied). You can include covariates for both levels of occupancy, which is nice if you think those relationships might change at different spatial scales.


But if that model won't work out for you, then the approach you described before (applying detection probability from this year to last year's data) seems good to me, but as you pointed out the big assumption there is that detection probability doesn't change among years.


Good Luck!

messages.author: e498b38f01df2491
messages.subject: Re: Marsh Seedeater occurrence study
parts:
Dear Joaquin,

Very interesting study!

I was just wondering about your replicates to estimate detection probability. I don't know this species, but maybe you might need to survey the temporal replicates very close in time to assure that you will estimate only detection probability. Otherwise this would be confounded with temporal emigration.
I work with dolphins, and as they present high mobility, we used a boat with observers in the bow and stern, so the duplicates are almost instantaneous. Maybe you can work with two teams (observers) at the same time (if this does not change birds behaviour and the observers are independent...). Just a thought!

All best,
Heloise
